profile.reading:
The New York Stock Exchange's primary data center sits on North Central Avenue in Mahwah, Bergen County, New Jersey. It is now owned and operated by Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), which acquired NYSE Euronext for approximately 8.2 billion dollars in a deal announced in December 2012 and completed the following year.

The Mahwah facility was built around five 20,000 square foot modular data halls, totaling roughly 100,000 square feet of raised floor space, inside a building with an overall footprint of about 400,000 square feet. Total power capacity is reported at 28 megawatts. The modules were brought online in stages over roughly two years in the period leading up to the ICE acquisition, as part of a broader consolidation of NYSE's technology footprint.

Before Mahwah, NYSE's trading and market data infrastructure was spread across eight data centers, six in the United States and two in Europe. The Mahwah build, alongside a companion site in Basildon, England, let the exchange shrink to two primary production data centers serving its global markets. Mahwah houses the electronic matching engines that execute trades on the New York Stock Exchange and other markets ICE operates, and it doubles as a colocation facility, renting rack and cage space to proprietary trading firms, market makers and brokers who want their servers physically close to the matching engines to minimize network latency. This low latency colocation business is a specialized niche within the data center industry, distinct from the general enterprise or cloud colocation offered by most commercial providers, and it has made Mahwah one of the most closely watched facilities in electronic trading since it opened.

Today the site operates under ICE's colocation and connectivity business, marketed as ICE Global Network and Colocation, which publishes technical specifications, cabinet options and network access details for prospective trading firms directly on its own site rather than through third party listing services. The facility's profile has made it a recurring subject of financial and technology press coverage, particularly around latency, market structure and high frequency trading, since the physical location of a trading firm's servers inside the Mahwah building can measurably affect execution speed relative to competitors.

Public information about Mahwah is unusually detailed for a data center, a reflection of ICE's own published specifications for its colocation customers rather than third party estimation. Granular operational details such as current tenant occupancy or specific future expansion plans beyond the original five module build are not published.

reading.body:
The Mahwah facility is a 28 megawatt data center in Bergen County, New Jersey, built and operated for electronic trading infrastructure. It comprises five 20,000 square foot modules totaling 100,000 square feet of data hall space within a 400,000 square foot building. The facility came online in stages before 2012 and is owned and operated by Intercontinental Exchange, Inc.

This campus ranks sixth among the five New Jersey facilities with published power figures, meaning its published capacity exceeds the state total of 111.3 megawatts when added. The operator's published specifications describe the facility as designed for colocation of high-frequency trading systems requiring low latency to exchange matching engines, a specialized use case distinct from general cloud or enterprise data center services. No published specifications describe IT load density, power consumption by use case, cooling systems, renewable energy sources, or grid interconnection points.

For AI deployment, this facility's relevance depends on undisclosed factors. The 28 megawatts total capacity, assuming 40 kilowatts per rack as a common AI training density, would support roughly 700 racks. The operator's technical specifications for prospective colocation tenants are not published here. Whether this campus can host or is currently hosting large-scale AI compute workloads is not stated in the available data.
